claim: CpxII is the only Cpx isoform expressed in mouse chromaffin cells.
source: CpxII is the only Cpx isoform expressed in mouse chromaffin cells (Cai et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cai et al., 2008.

claim: CpxII ko strongly reduced Ca2+-triggered synchronized vesicle fusion.
source: The results show that CpxII ko strongly reduced Ca2+-triggered synchronized vesicle fusion (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CpxII ko was accompanied by a profound increase in asynchronous exocytosis during the loading phase with NP-EGTA.
source: which was accompanied by a profound increase in asynchronous exocytosis during the loading phase with NP-EGTA (free [Ca]i~700 nM, Figure 1E and F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Expression of the wild-type CpxII protein fully restored the typical flash-evoked response with a prominent exocytotic burst.
source: Expression of the wild-type (WT) protein (CpxII ko+CpxII) fully restored the typical flash-evoked response with a prominent exocytotic burst (EB, Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of wild-type CpxII prevented any granule loss by premature exocytosis.
source: Expression of the wild-type (WT) protein (CpxII ko+CpxII) fully restored the typical flash-evoked response with a prominent exocytotic burst (EB, Figure 1B) and prevented any granule loss by premature exocytosis (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: CpxII hinders premature vesicle exocytosis that would otherwise outpace phasic secretion.
source: Thus, CpxII hinders premature vesicle exocytosis, that would otherwise outpace phasic secretion, agreeing with our previous observations (Dhara et al., 2014; Makke et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Dhara et al., 2014; Makke et al., 2018) and by inference from the experimental data.

claim: Both components of the exocytotic burst (RRP and SRP) were similarly affected by CpxII ko without altering the sustained rate of secretion.
source: Both components of the EB, the readily releasable pool (RRP) and the slowly releasable pool (SRP), were similarly affected, without altering the sustained rate (SR) of secretion (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Loss of CpxII conferred a slower time constant of the RRP response and a longer secretory delay.
source: Furthermore, loss of CpxII conferred a slower time constant of the RRP response and a longer secretory delay (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CpxII not only hinders premature secretion but also accelerates exocytosis timing.
source: Overall, CpxII not only hinders premature secretion but also accelerates exocytosis timing.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data showing effects on both premature secretion and exocytosis kinetics.

claim: The inhibitory function of CpxII resides within the last 34 amino acids of its CTD.
source: The inhibitory function of CpxII resides within the last 34 amino acids of its CTD (Makke et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Makke et al., 2018.

claim: The CTD of CpxII is characterized by an amphipathic helix and an upstream located cluster of glutamate residues.
source: which is characterized by an amphipathic helix and an upstream located cluster of glutamate residues (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the sequence information shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Truncation of the amphipathic helix (CpxII 1–115) strongly reduced the RRP component of the exocytotic burst.
source: Truncation of the amphipathic helix (CpxII 1–115) strongly reduced the RRP component of the EB (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Truncation of the amphipathic helix (CpxII 1–115) elevated premature secretion when compared with the WT protein.
source: Truncation of the amphipathic helix (CpxII 1–115) strongly reduced the RRP component of the EB (Figure 1B) and elevated premature secretion (Figure 1E and F) when compared with the WT protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The CpxII 1–115 amp helix mutant, in which the last 19 amino acids were replaced with an unrelated amphipathic helix, fully restored the flash-evoked response.
source: Surprisingly, the CpxII 1–115 amp helix mutant, in which the last 19 amino acids were replaced with an unrelated amphipathic helix (Figure 1A), fully restored the flash-evoked response and the ability of CpxII to prevent premature secretion (Figure 1B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-F.

claim: The CpxII 1–115 amp helix mutant fully restored the ability of CpxII to prevent premature secretion.
source: Surprisingly, the CpxII 1–115 amp helix mutant, in which the last 19 amino acids were replaced with an unrelated amphipathic helix (Figure 1A), fully restored the flash-evoked response and the ability of CpxII to prevent premature secretion (Figure 1B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-F.

claim: The CpxII NTD determines the stimulus-secretion coupling.
source: As the CpxII NTD determines the stimulus-secretion coupling (Dhara et al., 2014; Makke et al., 2018), both the RRP secretion kinetics and the secretory delay was fully rescued by the mutant variants (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dhara et al., 2014 and Makke et al., 2018.

claim: The amphipathic helix of CpxII's CTD is a key determinant for the protein to prevent premature secretion.
source: Therefore, the amphipathic helix of CpxII's CTD is a key determinant for the protein to prevent premature secretion.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data showing that an unrelated amphipathic helix can functionally replace the native CTD.

claim: Perturbation of the hydrophobic face of the CpxII CTD amphipathic helix by replacing L124 and L128 with glutamate residues mimicked the phenotype of the truncated CpxII 1–115 variant.
source: Perturbation of the hydrophobic face of the CpxII CTD amphipathic helix by replacing the two hydrophobic leucine amino acids L124 and L128 with charged glutamate residues (CpxII L124E-L128E) mimicked the phenotype of the truncated CpxII 1–115 variant (Figure 2A–C compare with Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The CpxII L124E-L128E mutant only partially restored the exocytotic burst.
source: The CpxII L124E-L128E mutant only partially restored the EB (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CpxII L124E-L128E mutant largely failed to clamp premature vesicle exocytosis.
source: The CpxII L124E-L128E mutant only partially restored the EB (Figure 2B) and largely failed to clamp premature vesicle exocytosis (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Replacing L124 and L128 with tryptophan residues (CpxII L124W-L128W) fully rescued the exocytotic burst size.
source: In contrast, replacing the same leucine residues with hydrophobic tryptophan amino acids (CpxII L124W-L128W) fully rescued the EB size (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The CpxII L124W-L128W mutant prevented premature exocytosis like WT CpxII.
source: In contrast, replacing the same leucine residues with hydrophobic tryptophan amino acids (CpxII L124W-L128W) fully rescued the EB size (Figure 2E), and prevented premature exocytosis like WT CpxII (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No changes in the kinetics of synchronized exocytosis were detected for the CpxII L124E-L128E or L124W-L128W mutant variants.
source: No changes in the kinetics of synchronized exocytosis were detected for either mutant variant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutating L117 and L121 to either glutamate or tryptophan confirmed that preservation of the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic helix is a prerequisite for arresting premature fusion.
source: In the same line, mutating L117 and L121 to either glutamate (CpxII L117E-L121E) or tryptophan (CpxII L117W-L121W) confirmed the result that preservation of the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic helix is a prerequisite for arresting premature fusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CpxII CTD shares a high degree of structural similarity with the C-terminal half of the SNAP25-SN1 domain.
source: We have previously pointed out that the CpxII CTD shares a high degree of structural similarity with the C-terminal half of the SNAP25-SN1 domain and showed that corresponding CpxII-SNAP25-SN1 chimeras (residues 44–77) fully restore the function in CpxII-deficient cell (Makke et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Makke et al., 2018.

claim: CpxII-SNAP25-SN1 chimeras (residues 44–77) fully restore the function in CpxII-deficient cells.
source: We have previously pointed out that the CpxII CTD shares a high degree of structural similarity with the C-terminal half of the SNAP25-SN1 domain and showed that corresponding CpxII-SNAP25-SN1 chimeras (residues 44–77) fully restore the function in CpxII-deficient cell (Makke et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Makke et al., 2018.

claim: The sequence comparison between CpxII CTD and SNAP-25-SN1 reveals similar or even identical amino acids on the polar side of the amphipathic helix.
source: In addition to the identical pattern of hydrophobic amino acids (heptad repeat), the sequence comparison between CpxII CTD and SNAP-25-SN1 reveals similar or even identical amino acids on the polar side of the amphipathic helix (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Point mutants D118A, Q129A, D130A, K133A showed no obvious phenotype in either synchronous or asynchronous secretion response.
source: However, none of these point mutants showed an obvious phenotype, neither in the synchronous nor in the asynchronous secretion response (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The double point mutant D118K-D130K had no serious functional consequences compared to the response with the WT protein.
source: Similarly, the double point mutant D118K-D130K, with an intended charge reversal, had no serious functional consequences compared to the response with the WT protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Preserving the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic helix at the end of the CTD of CpxII is necessary to prevent premature exocytosis.
source: Collectively, they indicate that preserving the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic helix at the end of the CTD of CpxII is necessary to prevent premature exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data showing that mutations on the hydrophobic face impair clamping function.

claim: The GST-CpxII CTD pulled down Synaptotagmin I, Syntaxin 1A, and traces of SynaptobrevinII from detergent extract of mouse brain.
source: While no binding to GST alone was observed, the GST-CpxII CTD pulled down Synaptotagmin I (SytI), Syntaxin 1A (Syx1), and traces of SynaptobrevinII (SybII) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CpxII CTD-SNARE interactions and binding to SytI were abolished for the CpxII CTD L124E-L128E mutant.
source: CpxII CTD-SNARE interactions and binding to SytI were abolished for the 'loss of clamp' mutant CpxII CTD L124E-L128E (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CpxII CTD-SNARE interactions and binding to SytI were preserved or even enhanced for the CpxII CTD L124W-L128W mutant protein.
source: In contrast, they were preserved or even enhanced for the CpxII CTD L124W-L128W mutant protein with undiminished 'clamp' function.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The CpxII 1–115 amphipathic helix mutant efficiently co-precipitated SytI, Syx1, and SybII.
source: Furthermore, the CpxII 1–115 amphipathic helix mutant efficiently co-precipitated SytI, Syx1, and SybII (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CpxII and its mutant variants co-localize with SybII like the WT protein, indicating unperturbed sorting to chromaffin granules and lipid binding.
source: Accompanying immunofluorescence analyses reveal similar expression levels for CpxII and its mutant variants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and show that the latter co-localize with SybII like the WT protein, indicating unperturbed sorting to chromaffin granules and lipid binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inhibition of premature exocytosis by CpxII CTD and its mutants correlates with their ability to interact with SytI and SNARE proteins.
source: Taken together, the inhibition of premature exocytosis by CpxII CTD and its mutants correlates with their ability to interact with SytI and SNARE proteins, suggesting that these interactions are a prerequisite for CpxII CTD to prevent premature exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the correlation between binding data and functional data.

claim: The region upstream to the amphipathic helix (amino acid position 100–115) is characterized by a cluster of glutamate residues (aa 108–114) which is conserved across the animal kingdom.
source: The region upstream to the amphipathic helix is characterized by a cluster of glutamate residues (aa 108–114) which is conserved across the animal kingdom and, according to biochemical experiments, may serve as a putative SytI interaction site (Tokumaru et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tokumaru et al., 2008.

claim: The glutamate cluster may serve as a putative SytI interaction site according to biochemical experiments.
source: The region upstream to the amphipathic helix is characterized by a cluster of glutamate residues (aa 108–114) which is conserved across the animal kingdom and, according to biochemical experiments, may serve as a putative SytI interaction site (Tokumaru et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tokumaru et al., 2008.

claim: The mutant CpxII E-A only supported a reduced synchronized exocytotic burst with a specifically reduced RRP.
source: When expressed in CpxII ko chromaffin cells, the mutant CpxII E-A (Figure 4A) only supported a reduced synchronized EB (Figure 4B) with a specifically reduced RRP (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The CpxII E-A mutant exhibited slower fusion kinetics for both phases of the synchronous exocytosis (RRP and SRP) and an increased stimulus-secretion delay.
source: In addition, the remaining EB exhibited slower fusion kinetics for both phases of the synchronous exocytosis, the RRP and the SRP, and an increased stimulus-secretion delay when compared to the secretion response of WT CpxII (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Premature exocytosis was effectively suppressed by the CpxII E-A mutant.
source: Nevertheless, premature exocytosis was effectively suppressed by the CpxII E-A mutant, as was observed for the WT protein (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: No comparable slowing of exocytosis was observed when both the glutamate cluster and the amphipathic helix were truncated (CpxII 1–100 mutant).
source: Notably, no comparable slowing of exocytosis was observed when both protein domains, the glutamate cluster and the amphipathic helix, were truncated, such as with the CpxII 1–100 mutant (Makke et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Makke et al., 2018.

claim: With an intact CTD of CpxII, the glutamate cluster may be required as a contact site for SytI to release the molecular clamp of the downstream amphipathic helix.
source: Thus, with an intact CTD of CpxII, the glutamate cluster may be required as a contact site for SytI to release the molecular clamp of the downstream amphipathic helix and thus to trigger the rapid secretion response.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Loss of SytI reduced the exocytotic burst size, specifically by decreasing the RRP component.
source: Consistent with previous work (Voets et al., 2001; Nagy et al., 2006; Dhara et al., 2014), loss of SytI reduced the EB size, specifically by decreasing the RRP component (Figure 5A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C and citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of SytI prolonged the kinetics of SRP secretion as well as the secretory delay.
source: Consistent with previous work (Voets et al., 2001; Nagy et al., 2006; Dhara et al., 2014), loss of SytI reduced the EB size, specifically by decreasing the RRP component (Figure 5A–C), and prolonged the kinetics of SRP secretion as well as the secretory delay when compared to the WT response (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and citations to previous work.

claim: Additional loss of SytI in the absence of CpxII did not further aggravate the phenotype.
source: In stark contrast, additional loss of SytI in the absence of CpxII did not further aggravate the phenotype, suggesting that all SytI functions are critically dependent on the presence of CpxII.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data comparing single and double knockouts.

claim: All SytI functions are critically dependent on the presence of CpxII.
source: In stark contrast, additional loss of SytI in the absence of CpxII did not further aggravate the phenotype, suggesting that all SytI functions are critically dependent on the presence of CpxII.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: SytI deficiency did not alter premature secretion when compared to the response of WT cells or with the elevated secretion in the absence of CpxII.
source: Furthermore, SytI deficiency did not alter premature secretion when compared to the response of WT cells or with the elevated secretion in the absence of CpxII (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Changes in the CpxII expression systematically altered the amount of premature secretion, which inversely correlated with the exocytotic burst size.
source: At submicromolar [Ca]i, changes in the CpxII expression systematically altered the amount of premature secretion, which inversely correlated with the EB size (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CpxII inhibits premature secretion that would otherwise outpace synchronous release.
source: Thus, CpxII inhibits premature secretion that would otherwise outpace synchronous release.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the inverse correlation between premature secretion and burst size.

claim: CpxII hinders premature secretion in a SytI-independent manner.
source: A similar relationship between tonic secretion and EB size was found in the absence of SytI, indicating that CpxII hinders premature secretion in a SytI-independent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is an inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genetic loss of Syt7 reduced the exocytotic burst size.
source: Genetic loss of Syt7 also reduced the EB size (Figure 5G and H), agreeing with previous work (Schonn et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H and a citation to Schonn et al., 2008.

claim: Both components of the exocytotic burst (RRP and SRP) were similarly affected by loss of SytVII.
source: Both components of the EB, the RRP and the SRP, were similarly affected (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The RRP kinetics were found to be slightly faster in SytVII ko cells when compared with controls.
source: The RRP kinetics were found to be slightly faster when compared with controls (Figure 5I (inset), J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: Deletion of SytVII in the CpxII ko background almost completely eliminated the exocytotic burst, leaving only a sustained phase of secretion.
source: Strikingly, deletion of SytVII in the CpxII ko background almost completely eliminated the EB, leaving only a sustained phase of secretion behind (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: The phenotype of the CpxII-SytVII dko is remarkably similar to the compound deficiency of SytI and SytVII.
source: The phenotype of the CpxII-SytVII dko is remarkably similar to the compound deficiency of SytI and SytVII (Schonn et al., 2008), corroborating the view that CpxII serves as a gatekeeper of SytI function in the Ca2+-triggered exocytosis of chromaffin granules.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the comparison of phenotypes and is supported by a citation to Schonn et al., 2008.

claim: CpxII serves as a gatekeeper of SytI function in the Ca2+-triggered exocytosis of chromaffin granules.
source: The phenotype of the CpxII-SytVII dko is remarkably similar to the compound deficiency of SytI and SytVII (Schonn et al., 2008), corroborating the view that CpxII serves as a gatekeeper of SytI function in the Ca2+-triggered exocytosis of chromaffin granules.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: CpxII expression in SytVII ko cells enhances exocytosis like in WT cells.
source: In the same line, CpxII expression in SytVII ko cells enhances exocytosis like in WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: SytVII deficiency strongly reduced premature secretion when compared with WT cells or on the background of CpxII deficiency.
source: In contrast to the loss of SytI, SytVII deficiency strongly reduced premature secretion when compared with WT cells or on the background of CpxII deficiency (Figure 6K and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6K and L (note: the text references Figure 6K and L, but the figure numbering appears to be Figure 5K and L based on the context).

claim: Deletion of Syt VII profoundly alters the exocytotic rates at submicromolar [Ca2+]i.
source: Thus, deletion of Syt VII profoundly alters the exocytotic rates at submicromolar [Ca2+]i, a notion that agrees with its proposed function as high-affinity Ca2+ sensor (MacDougall et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data and is supported by a citation to MacDougall et al., 2018.

claim: While function of SytI is critically dependent on CpxII, SytVII appears to act independently, most likely in the Ca2+-dependent priming reaction.
source: Overall, the combined set of data reveals a differential interplay between the two Syt isoforms and CpxII. While function of SytI is critically dependent on CpxII, SytVII appears to act independently, most likely in the Ca2+-dependent priming reaction (Tawfik et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data and is supported by a citation to Tawfik et al., 2021.

claim: Overexpression of either WT CpxII or the mutant CpxII ΔN had no effect on the kinetics of exocytosis in cells lacking SytI.
source: Overexpression of either WT CpxII or the mutant CpxII ΔN had no effect on the kinetics of exocytosis in cells lacking SytI (Figure 6A–C), which demonstrates that CpxII requires SytI to accelerate exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: CpxII requires SytI to accelerate exocytosis.
source: Overexpression of either WT CpxII or the mutant CpxII ΔN had no effect on the kinetics of exocytosis in cells lacking SytI (Figure 6A–C), which demonstrates that CpxII requires SytI to accelerate exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: In SytVII ko cells, CpxII ΔN slowed down synchronous secretion and increased the secretory delay.
source: In contrast, in SytVII ko cells, CpxII ΔN slowed down synchronous secretion and increased the secretory delay (Figure 6D–F) as previously reported for overexpression in WT cells (Dhara et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-F and a citation to Dhara et al., 2014.

claim: Both CpxII and CpxII ΔN hindered premature exocytosis independent of the present Syt isoform.
source: Furthermore, both, CpxII and CpxII ΔN, hindered premature exocytosis independent of the present Syt isoform, corroborating the view that CpxII hinders SNARE action rather than blocking one of the main Ca2+ sensors in chromaffin cells (Figure 6E, F, K, and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E, F, K, and L.

claim: CpxII hinders SNARE action rather than blocking one of the main Ca2+ sensors in chromaffin cells.
source: Furthermore, both, CpxII and CpxII ΔN, hindered premature exocytosis independent of the present Syt isoform, corroborating the view that CpxII hinders SNARE action rather than blocking one of the main Ca2+ sensors in chromaffin cells (Figure 6E, F, K, and L).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: CpxII NTD and SytI are functionally interdependent in the activation of fast synchronous exocytosis.
source: Together, these findings support a scenario in which CpxII NTD and SytI are functionally interdependent in the activation of fast synchronous exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The CpxII NTD directly regulates SytI rather than acting as a molecular switch between Syt isoforms.
source: Because the CpxII ΔN mutant slows down secretion in SytVII ko cells as in WT cells (Dhara et al., 2014), the CpxII NTD directly regulates SytI rather than acting as a molecular switch between these Syt isoforms.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data and is supported by a citation to Dhara et al., 2014.

claim: The phenotype of the SytI R233Q ki mutant in chromaffin cells is kinetically similar to that of the CpxII ΔN mutant.
source: Intriguingly, the phenotype of the R233Q ki mutant in chromaffin cells is kinetically similar to that of the CpxII ΔN mutant, as it also slows down timing of exocytosis compared to WT cells (Sørensen et al., 2003; Dhara et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sørensen et al., 2003 and Dhara et al., 2014.

claim: The SytI R233Q mutation slowed down the rate of exocytosis, prolonged the secretory delay and enhanced the exocytotic burst size when compared to WT cells.
source: Consistent with previous work by Sørensen et al., 2003, we found that the SytI R233Q mutation slowed down the rate of exocytosis, prolonged the secretory delay and enhanced the EB size when compared to WT cells (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-D and a citation to Sørensen et al., 2003.

claim: Overexpression of the CpxII ΔN mutant in SytI R233Q ki cells further slowed down the rate of synchronized release and restored the exocytotic burst size to the WT level.
source: Overexpression of the CpxII ΔN mutant in SytI R233Q ki cells, which is expected to outcompete the function of endogenous CpxII in these cells (Dhara et al., 2014), further slowed down the rate of synchronized release and restored the EB size to the WT level (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D and a citation to Dhara et al., 2014.

claim: Overexpression of the WT CpxII significantly accelerated the kinetics of synchronous exocytosis in SytI R233Q ki cells, restoring them to the level of WT cells.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of the WT CpxII significantly accelerated the kinetics of synchronous exocytosis in SytI R233Q ki cells, restoring them to the level of WT cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: CpxII WT and its mutant showed an undiminished suppression of premature exocytosis in the SytI R233Q ki cells.
source: Furthermore, CpxII WT and its mutant showed an undiminished suppression of premature exocytosis in the SytI R233Q ki cells (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: CpxII with its NTD is able to compensate for the functional deficiencies of the SytI R233Q mutation.
source: Thus, CpxII with its NTD is able to compensate for the functional deficiencies of the SytI R233Q mutation.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data showing rescue of the R233Q phenotype by WT CpxII.

claim: Exocytosis timing in chromaffin cells is largely determined by the kinetics of Ca2+ binding to SytI.
source: Given that exocytosis timing in chromaffin cells is largely determined by the kinetics of Ca2+ binding to SytI (Voets et al., 2001; Sørensen et al., 2003), the opposite effects of the WT protein and its ΔN mutant on the kinetics of secretion indicate that the NTD of CpxII accelerates mechanisms regulated by the Ca2+-binding kinetics of SytI.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Voets et al., 2001 and Sørensen et al., 2003.

claim: The NTD of CpxII accelerates mechanisms regulated by the Ca2+-binding kinetics of SytI.
source: Given that exocytosis timing in chromaffin cells is largely determined by the kinetics of Ca2+ binding to SytI (Voets et al., 2001; Sørensen et al., 2003), the opposite effects of the WT protein and its ΔN mutant on the kinetics of secretion indicate that the NTD of CpxII accelerates mechanisms regulated by the Ca2+-binding kinetics of SytI.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data and established knowledge about Ca2+ binding kinetics.

claim: Overexpression of CpxII WT protein in SytI R233Q ki cells shifted the half-maximal concentration for pool depletion (P50) to lower [Ca]i.
source: Overexpression of CpxII WT protein in SytI R233Q ki cells clearly shifted the half-maximal concentration for pool depletion (P50) to lower [Ca]i, whereas overexpression of the CpxII ΔN mutant increased it (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Overexpression of the CpxII ΔN mutant in SytI R233Q ki cells increased the half-maximal concentration for pool depletion (P50).
source: Overexpression of CpxII WT protein in SytI R233Q ki cells clearly shifted the half-maximal concentration for pool depletion (P50) to lower [Ca]i, whereas overexpression of the CpxII ΔN mutant increased it (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: WT CpxII rescued the secretion deficit of the Syt R233Q mutant.
source: Evidently, WT CpxII rescued the secretion deficit of the Syt R233Q mutant, as observed in the flash experiment (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: For the SytI R233Q ki cells, fusion rates increase as a function of [Ca]i and are shifted with similar slope to either lower [Ca2+]i (SytI R233Q+CpxII) or higher [Ca]i (SytI R233Q+CpxII ΔN), indicating unchanged cooperativity of Ca2+ binding.
